standards.name: MINSEQE
standards.abstract: MINSEQE (Minimum Information about a high-throughput Nucleotide SEQuencing Experiment) defines the minimum metadata that should accompany high-throughput sequencing (HTS) experiments — for example RNA-Seq, ChIP-Seq, DNA methylation assays — to enable unambiguous interpretation and reproduction. The standard, produced by the FGED Society (version 1.0, June 2012; Zenodo DOI available), outlines five essential elements to report: sample/biological-system annotation, raw sequence read data (with quality scores), final processed/summary data, general experiment information and sample-data relationships, and experimental plus data-processing protocols. Its scope is reporting requirements for HTS data submission and publication to improve reuse, integration across studies, and reproducibility.

classification.rationale: The source is organized as a short prose guideline with five numbered reporting elements (a checklist of what to report). It provides descriptive requirements rather than a field-level table or an ordered workflow, so it is best represented as a set of principles.

principles.principle: Description of the biological system, samples, and experimental variables
principles.evidence:
1. The description of the biological system, samples, and the experimental variables being studied.
Essential sample annotation, including the experimental factors and their values, must be given. Experimental factors are the key experimental variables, e.g. “compound” and “dose” in dose-­response experiments or “antibody” in ChIP-­‐Seq experiments. In addition to experimental factor values, essential information about the biological system from which samples were taken must be given, e.g. the organism, strain or cultivar (if known and if appropriate), the organism part or tissue, and what treatment(s) was/were applied.

principles.principle: Sequence read data for each assay (raw reads and quality scores)
principles.evidence: 2. The sequence read data for each assay. This represents the complete set of read sequences and base-­level quality scores for each assay, as generated by the sequencing instrument, in a recognized format. Currently FASTQ format is recommended, with a description of the scale used for quality scores.

principles.principle: Final processed (summary) data underlying study conclusions
principles.evidence: 3. The ‘final’ processed (or summary) data for the set of assays in the study. The final processed data is defined as the data on which the conclusions in the related publication are based. Currently there are no widely adopted formats for processed HTS data. Until such standardized formats become available, it is essential that descriptions of the data format be provided. For gene expression, in many cases these data can be presented as a matrix with each row corresponding to a genomic region (such as a gene or exon), each column representing a particular biological state (e.g. a time point in a time course experiment), and each element in the matrix representing a measurement of the particular genomic region in the particular biological state. Similarly, other applications like ChIP-­Seq analyses typically generate tabular output for identified peaks mapped to a reference sequence.

principles.principle: General information about the experiment and sample-data relationships
principles.evidence:
4. General information about the experiment and sample-­data relationships
General information about the overall study includes a summary of the experiment and its goals, contact information, and any associated publication. Part of this description should be a table specifying sample-­data relationships, i.e. which sample has led to which raw data file or which data element in the processed data files.

5. Essential experimental and data processing protocols
Experimental processing methods should describe how the nucleic acid samples were isolated, purified and processed prior to sequencing. As each of the different sequencing platforms use technologies that are based on highly divergent chemistries, it is recommended that a summary of the instrumentation used, library preparation strategy, labelling and amplification methodologies, alignment algorithms and data filtering used be provided. Data processing and analysis protocols must be described in sufficient detail to enable unambiguous data interpretation and to enable scientists to reproduce the analysis steps. This should include, but is not limited to, data rejection methods, data correction methods, alignment methods, data smoothing and filtering methods and identifiers used for reference genomes to which the sequences were mapped (when applicable).

standards.notes: Source: MINSEQE version 1.0 (June 2012) — FGED Society. The standard is a reporting checklist (not a field-level metadata table) intended to be used by journals, archives and curators; templates and checklists are recommended but not defined as concrete typed fields in the source.

standards.name: MIAME (Minimum Information About a Microarray Experiment)
standards.abstract: MIAME defines the minimum information that should be reported to enable interpretation and potential reproduction of microarray (and related high-throughput transcriptomic) experiments. It applies to experiments that measure gene expression or sequence-derived counts, covering raw data files (e.g., CEL, GPR, FASTQ), processed/normalized data matrices, sample annotations (tissue, sex, age, experimental factors), array/feature annotation (gene IDs, coordinates, probe sequences), experimental design relationships (which files correspond to which samples, replicate structure), and laboratory/data-processing protocols. The standard was originally published by Brazma et al. (2001) and has been maintained and promoted by the FGED community and repositories such as NCBI GEO; it addresses the problem of insufficient metadata accompanying microarray and sequencing submissions and provides a concise checklist of what information must be provided to make experiments interpretable and reusable.

classification.rationale: The source materials present MIAME as a checklist/list of minimum items to be reported (a set of reporting requirements), not as a structured metadata table or an ordered sequence of stages. Each item is an instruction about what information to provide (e.g., 'The raw data for each hybridisation'), so the actual structure is best represented as a set of principles.

principles.principle: Provide the raw data for each assay.
principles.evidence: The raw data for each hybridisation (e.g., CEL or GPR files)

principles.principle: Provide the final processed (normalized) data for the set of assays in the study.
principles.evidence: The final processed (normalised) data for the set of hybridisations in the experiment (study) (e.g., the gene expression data matrix used to draw the conclusions from the study)

principles.principle: Provide essential sample annotation including experimental factors and their values.
principles.evidence: The essential sample annotation including experimental factors and their values (e.g., compound and dose in a dose response experiment)

principles.principle: Describe the experimental design including sample–data relationships (which raw data file relates to which sample, replicate structure).
principles.evidence: The experimental design including sample data relationships (e.g., which raw data file relates to which sample, which hybridisations are technical, which are biological replicates)

principles.principle: Provide sufficient annotation of the array or sequence features examined (gene identifiers, coordinates, probe sequences or catalog numbers).
principles.evidence: Sufficient annotation of the array (e.g., gene identifiers, genomic coordinates, probe oligonucleotide sequences or reference commercial array catalog number)

principles.principle: Provide the essential laboratory and data-processing protocols (e.g., normalization methods used).
principles.evidence: The essential laboratory and data processing protocols (e.g., what normalisation method has been used to obtain the final processed data)

standards.notes: Sources: FGED Society MIAME page and NCBI GEO MIAME guidance (GEO implements submission procedures to enable MIAME-compliant deposits). Original MIAME publication: Brazma et al. (2001).
